one_liner: Grammar-to-C++ parser generator for network protocols and file formats; Zeek's binpac successor, but slower than binpac on most microbenchmarks.
what_it_does: Spicy is a domain-specific language for attributed grammars (units, fields, hooks, &size/&until/&while attributes, regex fields, &synchronize error recovery) that the spicyc toolchain compiles through the HILTI intermediate language into C++. The output is either JIT-compiled .hlto shared objects loaded at startup, or generated C++ plus prototypes (parse1/parse2/parse3 entry points taking a hilti::rt::Stream) that a host application links against libhilti-rt and libspicy-rt. Zeek bundles it (since Zeek 5.0) so analyzers can be written as grammar plus an EVT file without C++; it is not source-compatible with binpac .pac grammars.
how_it_is_fast: Generated C++ is compiled with -O3 -DNDEBUG in release mode (spicy-config --cxxflags), after HILTI optimizer passes: control-flow-based dataflow with constant and copy propagation (default since 1.15), removal of unused struct fields and of unused filter/sink/random-access feature code, std::move insertion for last uses (1.17). Spicy 1.16 moved parsed unit instances onto the stack instead of the heap and trimmed parser state, which the release notes credit with 20-60% microbenchmark throughput gains; 1.17 inlined the waitForInput/atEod fast paths. Fixed-size bytes fields avoid per-byte work (100 MB BytesLength in 0.005 s, derived from page data), and regex fields run on the bundled justrx library; the speed story is incremental improvement of Spicy itself, not a technique that beats binpac.
when_to_use: Writing a new Zeek protocol or file analyzer without hand-written C++: grammar plus EVT file, events generated for you, shipped with Zeek.
Parsing untrusted binary network input where robustness matters more than peak throughput: generated code carries runtime checks and &synchronize-based error recovery.
Input that arrives in chunks of arbitrary size (reassembled TCP streams, large files): parsers suspend and resume incrementally instead of needing the whole buffer.

Grammars dominated by large bytes fields with &size or &until on a delimiter, where the 2025 harness shows Spicy at parity with binpac (BytesLength 0.005 s each) and binpac is only competitive when it uses bytestring rather than uint8[].
Standalone C++ tools that want a generated, type-safe parser for a binary file format via spicyc -x and the parse1/parse2 prototypes.
when_not_to_use: Hot paths made of many tiny nested units or records: WithUnit took 14.087 s vs binpac's 3.809 s and WithUnitSwitch 17.232 s vs 4.128 s on 100 MB (2025 harness), and still about 2x behind after the 1.16 improvements per the 2026 zeek.org post (snippet only).
Regex-heavy parsing of large payloads: /A*/ over 100 MB took 10.228 s vs 0.378 s for binpac's Zeek RE_Matcher (about 27x); a character class took 13.5 s on the same input.

When the goal is maximum raw throughput versus a hand-written C++ parser: no measurement against hand-written parsers exists, and the runtime carries fibers, hooks and location tracking that binpac and hand-written code do not.

Deployments that cannot ship a C++ compiler or tolerate long build times when using JIT: 80-90% of compile time is spent compiling generated C++; precompile HLTOs or generate C++ ahead of time instead.
Windows production use: MSVC support is community-contributed and not an officially supported platform.

integration.form: code generator (spicyc) plus runtime libraries: generated C++ linked against libhilti-rt/libspicy-rt, or JIT-compiled .hlto shared objects; built into Zeek
integration.dependencies: Toolchain build: CMake >= 3.15, Bison >= 3.0, Flex >= 2.6, Zlib; bundled 3rdparty justrx regex library; JIT mode needs a C++ compiler at runtime
integration.min_toolchain: C++20 (generated code compiled with -std=c++20); Clang >= 9 or GCC >= 12 per the installation docs
integration.platforms: Linux and macOS (source, Homebrew, Zeek Docker images; binary packages were removed); Windows/MSVC unofficial; fiber runtime enabled on PowerPC64 in 1.17
integration.thread_safety: Parsers can run concurrently in separate threads (README: 'potentially highly concurrently'), but 1.17 fixed a Fiber constructor race on the shared stack (GH-2354) and a data race on the checkStack counter, so use 1.17+ for multithreaded hosts; Spicy global variables are process-wide (FAQ).

gotchas: Harness flaw behind the catalogue numbers: run-benchmark.rb builds the Spicy side with spicy-config --cxxflags, which emits -O3 -DNDEBUG (hilti/toolchain/src/config.cc.in), but the binpac side with a bare 'clang++ ../bench_binpac.cc ...' and no -O flag, so it is Spicy -O3 against binpac -O0; Spicy's 3.7x-4.2x unit losses understate the gap to an optimized binpac.

The only Spicy win (BytesUntil 0.286 s vs 1.635 s) compares unlike grammars: Spicy parses 'bytes &until=b"B"' while binpac/bytes_until.pac parses 'uint8[] &until($element == 66)', a per-element vector; the harness README itself says binpac with bytestring is 'roughly the same as Spicy'. The committed bench.cc also fills its input with 'Z' while the README table was measured on 'A's, and the While (&while=$$=='A') and Regex (/A*/) units then need a 'B' terminator, so as committed those rows should hit a parse error (inferred from the grammar, not run); the binpac regex row came from a separate Zeek plugin not in the repo, with a patched Compile() call.
Regex fields capture by default; issue #1986 reports &nosub cutting the /A*/ case from about 10 s to about 3 s, still several times binpac's 0.3 s.

Since 1.16 units live on the stack and the optimizer drops struct fields no Spicy code reads: very large units can exhaust the fiber stack (declare them &on-heap, 1.17), and host code reading a field may find it '(optimized out)' unless the type is declared export or compiled with --strict-public-api.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Spicy over re2c or lexy only when the input is a binary network protocol or file format that needs incremental, robust parsing and Zeek integration; for raw C++ lexing or parsing throughput re2c (vs Ragel) and lexy (vs PEGTL) are the measured-faster choices, and Spicy itself is slower than its own baseline.
verified_claims_summary: In evantypanski/spicy-performance (Feb-Apr 2025, std::clock CPU seconds for one parse of a 100 MB synthetic input, mean of 5, no CPU or compiler version stated) Spicy built at -O3 tied binpac built at -O0 on BytesLength (0.005 s), won BytesUntil 0.286 vs 1.635 s only against a binpac uint8[] vector, and lost WithUnit 14.087 vs 3.809 s, WithUnitSwitch 17.232 vs 4.128 s and Regex 10.228 vs 0.378 s. The 2026 zeek.org follow-up (snippet only) reports the unit cases about 1.6x faster than a year earlier, consistent with seconds (WithUnit 9.357, WithUnitSwitch 11.061; 1.51x and 1.56x derived from page data) but still about 2x behind binpac's 4.663 and 4.866.
status_note: Actively maintained by the Zeek project (1.18.0-dev.37 on 2026-09-24, 1.17 released, CodSpeed-tracked Spicy-only microbenchmarks in spicy/runtime/tests/benchmarks) and BSD-licensed, but this entry documents a not-faster result: the only reachable Spicy-vs-binpac harness pits -O3 Spicy against -O0 binpac and shows Spicy slower on units, switches and regex.
